title: The Last Grand Master — Molay to the Fire on the Île aux Juifs
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Molay — the village in the County of Burgundy
stops.campa: In the wooded march of the Franche-Comté, under the Empire and not the crown of France, a son is born to the minor nobility at Molay. The land is poor, the winters hard, the horizon closed by the ridges of the Amont. He grows a boy of the frontier, hearing at Mass and market of the far kingdom across the sea, of Jerusalem lost and won and lost again, of the white mantle with the red cross that a man may earn if he give up all he has. The call is already in the air of the country before he knows his own name for it.
suggested_refs: The commune of Molay, Haute-Saône, claimed as his birthplace
The arms attributed to Jacques de Molay
sources: Alain Demurger, The Last Templar: The Tragedy of Jacques de Molay

stops.name: Beaune — the reception in the chapel of the Temple
stops.campa: By night, in the chapel of the Temple house at Beaune, Jacques is received into the Order of the Poor Knights of Christ. Humbert de Pairaud, Visitor of France and England, receives him; Amaury de la Roche, Master of France, stands by. He kneels, asks the bread and water of the house and the company of the brethren, and swears the threefold vow — poverty, chastity, obedience. They lay the white mantle with its red cross upon his shoulders and give him the kiss of peace. From this night he owns nothing; he is a soldier of God and the Temple until death.
stops.quote: I was received at Beaune, in the diocese of Autun, by Brother Humbert de Pairaud, in the presence of Brother Amaury de la Roche and others.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jacques de Molay, papal inquest (as recorded in the trial proceedings)
suggested_refs: The Rule of the Temple (Latin and French Rule)
The Temple commandery seal of Humbert de Pairaud
sources: Malcolm Barber, The Trial of the Templars

segments.name: Outremer — the Templar in the last of the Holy Land

stops.name: Acre — the Templar quarter in the last capital of the Kingdom
stops.campa: Molay crosses the sea to Outremer, to Acre, the last great city of the Christian East, where the Temple holds its strongest house behind the sea wall at the western tip. The kingdom of Jerusalem is a kingdom without Jerusalem now — a strip of coast, a scatter of castles, a truce always breaking. He serves in the ranks of the white knights through twenty years the chronicles scarcely record: garrison, patrol, the long dwindling of the Frankish East as Baibars and then Qalawun take the inland fortresses one by one. He learns the Order as a fighting brotherhood in its own last country.
suggested_refs: The ruins of the Templar tunnel and fortress at Acre (Akko)
Map of Frankish Acre and the military-order quarters

stops.name: Château Pèlerin (Atlit) — the great sea-castle of the Temple
stops.campa: South of Acre the Temple holds its mightiest fortress, Château Pèlerin — Atlit, the Pilgrim's Castle — thrust into the sea on its own headland, walls the Saracen never storms. Here and at Sidon, at Tortosa and Beirut, the white knights keep the shrinking coast. Molay comes up through the Order's inner councils in these years, a man of the frontier who has seen from a rampart the whole Frankish East pared back to a rind of shore. When Acre falls, Atlit will hold a few weeks more, then be abandoned to the waves — the last castle given up without a siege.
suggested_refs: Château Pèlerin (Atlit) fortress ruins, Israel
The Templar castles of the Latin coast

stops.name: Acre — the walls breached, the Gate of Saint Anthony
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of May the Mamluk host of al-Ashraf Khalil pours through the breached Accursed Tower. Grand Master Guillaume de Beaujeu, roused from sleep, gathers his knights and rides into the storm at the Gate of Saint Anthony. An arrow finds the gap in his mail beneath the raised arm; his men cry that he flees, and turning he shows them the shaft. 'I am not fleeing,' he answers, 'I am dead. See the blow.' They bear him back to die within the Temple. The city is lost; the streets run with the fall of two hundred years of the Christian kingdom of the East.
stops.quote: I am not fleeing; I am dead. Behold the blow.
stops.quote_source: The 'Templar of Tyre' (Gestes des Chiprois), on the death of Guillaume de Beaujeu
suggested_refs: The 'Templar of Tyre' manuscript (Gestes des Chiprois)
The Accursed Tower and the walls of Acre

stops.name: Acre — the last stand of the Temple by the sea, the flight to the ships
stops.campa: The city falls, but the seaward Temple fortress with its four towers holds days more, crowded with knights and thousands of the terrified. Marshal Peter de Sevrey commands the last stand. Offered safe passage, he sends the women and children to the galleys; when the Mamluks break faith and lay hands on them, the brothers shut the gates and fight. Sevrey, going out under truce to the Sultan's tent, is beheaded. On the twenty-eighth the undermined wall collapses; the Saracens rush the breach and the last Templars die in the ruin. Small boats pull for Cyprus over a red harbour. Outremer is finished.
suggested_refs: The seaward Templar castle of Acre (site)
The fall of Acre depicted in Dominique Papety, 'Guillaume de Clermont defending Ptolémaïs'

stops.name: Sidon — the sea-castle abandoned, the coast given up
stops.campa: In the weeks after Acre the whole Latin shore falls without a fight. The Templars hold Sidon a little while — the sea-castle on its causeway, the last refuge of the Marshal and the Grand Master's own household — then, hopeless of relief, put out for Cyprus and leave it to the Mamluk. Tortosa and Atlit follow before summer's end; the pilgrim castles that stood two hundred years are emptied to the tide. Molay lives through the extinction of Outremer itself: not one stone of the Kingdom of Jerusalem left in Christian hands on the mainland.
suggested_refs: The Sea Castle of Sidon (Saïda), Lebanon
The abandoned Templar castles of the Latin coast, 1291

segments.name: The Order in Exile — Cyprus and the White Mantle Grand Master

stops.name: Limassol — the Temple's headquarters in exile
stops.campa: The remnant of the Order gathers at Limassol on Cyprus, the new head of a house without a homeland. The white banner still flies, but over a garrison island, not a kingdom. In the chapter that follows, Molay speaks for reform — discipline restored, the treasury husbanded, the eyes of the brethren kept fixed on the coast they have lost. The Grand Master Thibaud Gaudin, who carried the Order's treasure out of Acre, does not long survive. The brethren look to the hard veteran of the Franche-Comté.
suggested_refs: Limassol Castle, Cyprus
The Templar and Hospitaller commanderies of Cyprus

stops.name: Limassol — elected Grand Master of the Temple
stops.campa: Sometime before the twentieth of April, the chapter elects Jacques de Molay the twenty-third and last Grand Master of the Poor Knights of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon. He takes up an office three centuries deep — the seal of the two knights on one horse, the beauceant banner, the obedience of thousands from Cyprus to the Atlantic. His charge is plain and, as it will prove, impossible: to hold the Order together and win back the Holy Land. He will spend the rest of his life at both, and be granted neither.
suggested_refs: The seal of the Grand Masters of the Temple (two knights, one horse)
The Beauceant, the black-and-white war banner
sources: Malcolm Barber, The Trial of the Templars

stops.name: Nicosia — the Temple against the King of Cyprus
stops.campa: In the little kingdom that is now his whole ground, Molay guards the Order's liberties against the Lusignan crown. King Henry II would bind the great orders to his will; the Grand Master, back from the West, defends the Temple's privileges as jealously as he defends the coast. When the crown itself is torn between Henry and his brother Amaury of Tyre, the Templars stand with Amaury, who seizes power and sends the king into exile. It is a hard, worldly stewardship — an order of warrior-monks entangled in the feuds of a Frankish island, keeping its strength intact for the reconquest still dreamed of.
suggested_refs: The Lusignan royal arms of Cyprus
Medieval Nicosia, capital of the Lusignan kingdom

segments.name: The Vain Reconquest — Ruad and the Coast Not Regained

stops.name: Famagusta — the fleet sails to raid the Syrian coast
stops.campa: From Famagusta sixteen galleys stand out to sea under Admiral Baudouin de Picquigny, Templars and Hospitallers and the men of Cyprus aboard. They fall upon the Egyptian and Syrian shore — Rosetta, Alexandria, the wreck of Acre, Tortosa, Maraclea — burning and taking spoil, holding nothing. It is a raid, not a return, and Molay knows it. But word runs through Christendom that the Mongol Ilkhan Ghazan will come down from the north against the Mamluk, and the Grand Master stakes the Order's strength on the hope of that alliance from the East.
suggested_refs: Famagusta, medieval harbour of Cyprus
Letters of Ghazan Ilkhan to the West on a joint crusade

stops.name: Tortosa — the raid on the mainland, the Mongol who never comes
stops.campa: The great design of Molay's grand-mastership hangs on the Mongols of Persia. If Ghazan the Ilkhan comes down through Syria against the Mamluk, the Cypriot host and the military orders will land on the coast and take Tortosa, and the Holy Land is opened again. An ambassador of Ghazan sails with the raiders; the Grand Master lands men on the Syrian shore and waits. But the Mongols come late or not at all — turned back, beaten at Homs and at Shaqhab south of Damascus. The Franks hold the beach a season and re-embark. The alliance from the East, prayed for through years, dissolves like a mirage.
suggested_refs: The cathedral-fortress of Tortosa (Tartus), Syria
Ghazan Ilkhan's crusading correspondence with the West

stops.name: Ruad — the island bridgehead off Tortosa
stops.campa: Two miles off Tortosa, Molay plants the Order's last foothold on the very edge of the Holy Land: the little island of Ruad. Pope Boniface grants it to the Temple; the brethren raise the walls and hold it with a hundred and twenty knights, five hundred archers, four hundred servants, under the Marshal Barthélemy de Quincy. From this rock they will step ashore the day the Mongols come. Molay sails back and forth, presses the West, keeps the bridgehead supplied across the winter sea. The horsemen of Ghazan, promised year on year, never appear.
suggested_refs: Arwad (Ruad) island fortress, Syria
The bull of Boniface VIII granting Ruad to the Temple (1301)

stops.name: Ruad — starved out, the last bridgehead lost
stops.campa: In 1302 the Mamluk fleet comes from Egypt by way of Tripoli — sixteen ships, an army disembarked at two points on the little island. The Templars fight, but there is no relief, no Mongol, no sea road left open, and hunger does what the assault cannot. On the twenty-sixth of September Brother Hugh of Dampierre parleys a surrender on terms of safe passage. The terms are broken as they step out: Marshal Barthélemy de Quincy is cut down, the archers and native Christian foot slaughtered to a man, the surviving knights dragged in chains to Cairo. The last inch of the Holy Land is gone.
suggested_refs: Arwad island, the last Crusader-held ground in the Levant
Mamluk accounts of the siege of Arwad

segments.name: The Diplomacy of the West — the Grand Master among the Kings

stops.name: Rome — the court of Pope Boniface VIII
stops.campa: Molay comes to the West on a long embassy for the crusade. He is present at the election of Boniface VIII, and lays before the Papacy the case of the Order and the recovery of the Holy Land — supplies for Cyprus, ships for the coast, a great host to be preached. He wins privileges, licences to export arms and grain past the ban on trade with the infidel, warm words. He wins no army. Christendom has turned inward; the kings war with each other; the fervour that raised the First Crusade is two centuries cold.
suggested_refs: The bronze effigy of Boniface VIII, Arnolfo di Cambio
The Lateran Palace, seat of the papal court

stops.name: Naples — the court of Charles II, ships for the crusade
stops.campa: At the Angevin court of Naples, Charles II — heir to the old claims on the East, kinsman to the fallen kingdom of Jerusalem — receives the Grand Master with honour. Here if anywhere the crusading fire might still be blown alight; here Molay presses for galleys, for a marriage of Angevin ambition to the Order's swords. He gathers promises and licences, alliances of paper. But Sicily is in revolt, France and Aragon at his host's throat, and the passage overseas slips again into the future. The Temple's Grand Master courts every prince who might sail east, and sails home alone.
suggested_refs: Castel Nuovo, Naples, seat of the Angevin kings
The Angevin claim to the Kingdom of Jerusalem

stops.name: London — the plea to Edward I of England
stops.campa: Grand Master of an order rich in every Christian realm, Molay journeys to the courts of the West — to Edward I of England, to James of Aragon, to Charles of Naples — pressing for men, money, and the leave to ship supplies east. He convenes the Order's own general chapters at Montpellier and Arles to set the house in order. Everywhere he is received with honour as a great lord of Christendom; everywhere the answer to a new crusade is the same soft deferral. The Temple is welcome at every table and answered by none.
suggested_refs: The New Temple, London (Temple Church)
Templar charters in the English royal archives

stops.name: Barcelona — the court of Aragon, licences to arm the East
stops.campa: To the Crown of Aragon, seasoned in war against the Moor and rich in Templar houses, Molay brings the same plea and wins the same partial grace: leave to buy horses and arms and ship grain to Cyprus in defiance of the trade-ban with the infidel. The kings will help the Order breathe; they will not raise the great passage overseas. Molay gathers what he can — supplies, novices, silver from the western commanderies — and turns it all toward the island and the coast. He is building an army for a war no king in the West any longer means to fight.
suggested_refs: The royal Aragonese Templar houses (Miravet, Peníscola)
Charters of James II of Aragon to the Temple

stops.name: Marseille — landing in France, summoned to the Pope
stops.campa: Leaving Cyprus on the fifteenth of October 1306, the Grand Master crosses to the West one last time, landing in Provence and coming up through France to answer the Pope's summons. He brings, the chroniclers say, a great train and much treasure — the outward sign of the Order's undiminished wealth, the very wealth that draws the King's eye. He does not know he is walking into the net. He comes as a prince of the Church-militant to counsel a crusade; he will not leave France alive.
suggested_refs: Medieval port of Marseille
The Grand Master's retinue and treasure entering France (chronicle accounts)

stops.name: Poitiers — before Clement V, and the refused merger
stops.campa: Summoned by the new Pope Clement V to counsel a fresh crusade and the union of the two military orders, Molay sails from Cyprus in October 1306 and comes into France. He writes his memorandum against the merger of Temple and Hospital: two orders in rivalry, he argues, are stronger and readier than one. He rebuts, too, the whispers already loud against his brethren, and asks the Pope himself for an inquiry to clear the Order's name. Clement, sickly and hemmed by the King of France, agrees to look into it. Molay believes the matter closing. It is opening.
stops.quote: Two orders, kept apart and in emulation of one another, will always be readier and better armed for the service of the Holy Land than one order alone.
stops.quote_source: Paraphrase of Molay's memorandum to Clement V against the union of the Orders (1306)
suggested_refs: Molay's memorandum on the crusade and the union of the Orders
The papal palace at Poitiers
sources: Malcolm Barber, The Trial of the Templars

segments.name: The Temple of Paris — the Fortress and the Dawn Raid

stops.name: Paris — the Enclos du Temple, banker to the crown
stops.campa: In Paris rises the Temple's greatest house in the West — the walled Enclos, and over it the Great Tower, the Donjon, tallest thing in the city, holding the treasury of France itself. Here the crown keeps its revenues; here the debt-drowned Philip the Fair has borrowed deep from the poor knights he cannot repay. On the feast of Saint John, Molay meets the King in Paris over the rumours against the Order and comes away half reassured. He does not read the King's true account: an emptied treasury, a coveted hoard, and a plan already sealed.
suggested_refs: The Tower of the Temple (Donjon), Paris, later prison of Louis XVI
The Square du Temple, on the site of the Enclos

stops.name: Paris — the funeral of Catherine of Courtenay, the eve
stops.campa: On the twelfth of October the Grand Master walks in honour as a pallbearer at the funeral of Catherine of Courtenay, sister-in-law of the King — a prince of the Church-militant at the heart of the royal court, trusted, esteemed, unsuspecting. That very day, across the whole realm of France, sealed royal letters lie already in the hands of the King's officers, to be opened at dawn. They command a single act, everywhere at once. Molay goes to his bed in the Temple a great lord. It is his last night as a free man.
suggested_refs: The sealed arrest order of Philip IV (14 September 1307)
Catherine of Courtenay, titular Empress of Constantinople

stops.name: Paris — Friday, 13 October 1307, the Temple taken
stops.campa: At dawn on Friday the thirteenth of October the sealed orders open in every bailiwick of France, and in a single morning the King's men fall upon every house of the Temple. In Paris they take the Enclos and its Grand Master; near seven score brethren are seized in the capital alone, thousands across the kingdom, the strongest order in Christendom broken in one stroke without a sword drawn against it. Molay, who has faced the Mamluk in the breach of Acre, is put in irons by the officers of the king he served as banker. The charge is heresy.
stops.quote: God is not pleased. We have enemies of the faith in the kingdom.
stops.quote_source: Opening of Philip IV's arrest order to the bailiffs and seneschals of France (14 September 1307)
suggested_refs: Friday the 13th and the arrest of the Templars in tradition
The royal writ of arrest read out across France

segments.name: The Trial — Torture, Confession, and Retraction

stops.name: Paris — the interrogation and the wrung confession
stops.campa: Within days, under the inquisitors and the shadow of the rack, the confessions come. The charges are monstrous: that at reception the brethren denied Christ, spat upon or beside the cross, exchanged obscene kisses, and adored an idol — a bearded head, the thing the accusers name Baphomet. On the twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth of October the Grand Master himself confesses to the denial and the spitting, and is made to write to all his brethren bidding them confess likewise. The Order's own head has been turned against it. Torture has done in a fortnight what the Saracen could not do in a lifetime.
stops.quote: He confessed that, at his reception, he had denied Christ and had spat upon the cross set before him.
stops.quote_source: Trial proceedings, Paris interrogation of Jacques de Molay, 24–25 October 1307
suggested_refs: The Baphomet idol of the charges (later Lévi/Eliphas imagery)
The instruments of the medieval inquisition

stops.name: Chinon — questioned before the cardinals, the absolution
stops.campa: In the great fortress on the Vienne, three cardinals sent by Clement V examine the Order's leaders. On the twentieth of August Molay is brought last before them. The parchment records his confession and, over the spitting, the strange half-refusal remembered from his reception — that when bidden to spit on the cross he chose to spit beside it, fearing to defile the wood. Having abjured heresy and sworn upon the Gospel, he is absolved of excommunication and restored to the Church's communion. Between Pope and King the Grand Master is a coin passed back and forth, absolved in one court and doomed in another.
stops.quote: And since he feared the receptor would draw back his hand and some spittle fall upon the cross, he did not spit on the hand, but spat beside the cross.
stops.quote_source: The Chinon Parchment (record of the interrogation of Jacques de Molay, August 1308)
suggested_refs: The Chinon Parchment (Archivum Secretum Vaticanum)
The royal fortress of Chinon

stops.name: Paris — before the Papal Commission, the retraction
stops.campa: When the Papal Commission opens in Paris, Molay stands before it and takes back all he confessed. He will not acknowledge the crimes laid on his Order; he asks only to defend it, though he is no clerk and pleads his own poverty of learning against the trained doctors ranged against him. But the King has moved first and hard: in May of 1310, on the strength of the forced confessions, four and fifty Templars who dared retract are burned in a single day outside Paris. The lesson is not lost. The Grand Master falls silent, his defence choked in the smoke of his own brethren.
stops.quote: I am not learned enough to defend the Order as it deserves; I ask only to be heard, for the Order is pure and holy.
stops.quote_source: Reported testimony of Molay before the Papal Commission, Paris, November 1309 (paraphrase from the proceedings)
suggested_refs: The burning of fifty-four Templars outside Paris (1310)
The register of the Papal Commission of Paris

stops.name: Vienne — the Order suppressed, Vox in excelso
stops.campa: At the Council of Vienne, with Philip come in person to press the churchmen, Clement V dissolves the Order of the Temple — not by verdict of guilt, which the evidence will not bear, but by decree, for the scandal and infamy now clinging to its name. The bull Vox in excelso, 'A voice from on high,' ends two hundred years of the Poor Knights of Christ at a stroke of the pen. Their lands are given to the Hospital; their leaders wait still in prison, their fate reserved to the Pope. Molay, uncondemned and unfreed, endures in the dark of his cell.
stops.quote: Vox in excelso audita est — A voice was heard from on high, of lamentation and bitter weeping.
stops.quote_source: Opening of the bull Vox in excelso, Clement V, 22 March 1312
suggested_refs: The bull Vox in excelso
The cathedral of Saint-Maurice, Vienne, seat of the Council

stops.name: Paris — the years in the dungeon
stops.campa: The Order is dead; its Grand Master is not. Uncondemned and unfreed, Molay lies year upon year in prison while the great men of the world settle the bones of the Temple — its lands to the Hospital, its treasure to the crown, its guilt or innocence to the reserved judgement of the Pope. He is near seventy now, the old soldier of Acre and Ruad, forgotten in the dark between the courts. He waits, an inconvenient survivor, until at last the King and the cardinals remember there is still a sentence to pronounce upon the last Master of the Temple.
suggested_refs: The Tower of the Temple, Paris, place of his imprisonment
The register of the Templar trials

segments.name: The Fire and the Curse — the Île aux Juifs

stops.name: Paris — the scaffold before Notre-Dame, the last recantation
stops.campa: Seven years in the dungeon, and on the eighteenth of March the cardinals mount a scaffold before Notre-Dame to pronounce the Grand Master and Geoffroi de Charney to perpetual imprisonment on their old confessions. Then, before the whole city, Molay and Charney rise and cry out that they are guilty of one thing only — of having betrayed their holy Order by confessing to lies to save their lives, under torture, to please the King. The Temple, they proclaim, is innocent and its rule pure. The prelates recoil; the King, hearing of it, orders them burned the same day as relapsed heretics.
stops.quote: We are not guilty of the crimes charged against us; but we are guilty of basely betraying our Order to save our lives. The Order is pure, it is holy; the accusations are lies.
stops.quote_source: Continuator of William of Nangis, Chronicle, on 18 March 1314
suggested_refs: The parvis of Notre-Dame de Paris
The Grandes Chroniques de France, miniature of the burning of the Templars

stops.name: Île aux Juifs — the fire, and the summons from the flames
stops.campa: At evening a pyre is raised on the little Île aux Juifs in the Seine, below Notre-Dame between the royal gardens and the city. Molay asks that his hands be freed to pray and his face turned toward the church of the Virgin, of whom Christ was born; it is granted. The slow fire takes him, and men marvel that he dies with such stillness. From the flames the Grand Master calls his judges to God's tribunal: within the year Pope Clement and King Philip shall answer there. Clement dies within the month; Philip before the year is out. The Capetian line withers — les rois maudits, the accursed kings.
stops.quote: God knows who is in the wrong and has sinned; misfortune will soon fall on those who have wrongly condemned us. God will avenge our death. I beseech you, turn my face toward the Virgin Mary, of whom our Lord Christ was born.
stops.quote_source: Geoffroi de Paris, Chronique métrique, eyewitness of the burning, 18 March 1314
suggested_refs: The plaque to Jacques de Molay on the Pont Neuf near the Square du Vert-Galant (site of the Île aux Juifs)
Maurice Druon, Les Rois maudits (The Accursed Kings)
